Kepler’s Laws

A fun, interactive walk-through of all three of Kepler’s Laws.

Kepler’s First Law: Derivation

Abir Mehta

1. What is Kepler’s 1st Law?

The first of Kepler’s laws states that the orbit of a planet around its Sun generates an elliptical path, with the Sun at one of the foci of the ellipse.

By the way, if you are unfamiliar with ellipses and their respective terminology (which we will be discussing in detail throughout this law), you should check out the Vectors & Ellipses section for appropriate background! We lean on that vocabulary constantly here, especially the semi-major axis $a$ and the eccentricity $e = c/a$.

2. How Do We Prove Kepler’s 1st Law?

2.1 Motives

Well, for most of us, this law is very hard to rigorously prove analytically. You would have to solve the differential equation of motion for the orbit’s radius as a function of its angle, and then show that what falls out of it is exactly the polar equation of an ellipse. That is well beyond the scope of our discussion (a phrase you’ve heard a few times by now). The entire derivation isn’t particularly challenging to think of, but simply mind-bendingly tedious with the amount of algebra you have to do, building up from nothing!

A simpler way to visualize this law is through the use of a computer simulation in Python, which is exactly what we will be doing on this page. We’ll show Kepler’s 1st Law, but in an entirely different way, which (in my opinion) can be just as rewarding.

Here’s the idea. We give a planet a starting position and a starting velocity, and we tell the computer exactly one physical rule: Newton’s law of gravitation. That’s the only rule it gets, and we say nothing at all about ellipses. Then we let it take thousands of tiny steps forward in time and plot every position the planet visits. If Kepler was right, an ellipse should show up on your screen with the Sun at a focus, purely because of the force law.

2.2 The Plan

Since this page is a bit longer than the other two laws, here’s where we’re going, so you know where each piece fits:

  1. The differential equation of motion, from Newton’s 2nd Law and the vector form of gravity. (Section 3)
  2. Initial conditions, so we get the one specific ellipse we asked for instead of some random orbit. (Section 4)
  3. The Vis-Viva equation, which tells us how hard to kick the planet. This is the only real derivation on the page. (Section 5)
  4. Euler’s method, which is how we get a computer to march the equation forward in time. (Section 6)

Then we build the code in Section 7 and run it.

3. The Differential Equation

The entire gist of proving Kepler’s 1st Law is showing how the differential equation of motion leads to the familiar ellipse. Now you may be asking: what differential equation of motion? We can develop it directly from Newton’s 2nd Law,

$$\sum \vec{F} = m\vec{a}.$$

We consider a planet of mass $m$ in orbit about a star of mass $M$, which sits at the origin $(0,0)$ of our Cartesian plane. I’m sure you guys know the magnitude representation of Newton’s law of gravitation:

$$F_g = \frac{GMm}{r^2},$$

where $G$ is the gravitational constant and $r$ is the distance between the two bodies. In vector form, which you met back on the 2nd Law page, we can write this as

$$\vec{F}_g = -\frac{GMm}{r^2}\, \hat{r}.$$

Here, $\hat{r}$ is a unit vector that points along the line connecting the two bodies, and the negative sign simply indicates that the force of gravity is inward, relative to the origin. Refer to the Vectors & Ellipses section (or the 2nd Law page) if any part of this confuses you.

We assume that the planet is given some initial tangential velocity so that it sets into a stable orbit. The only force that acts on the planet is the gravitational force $\vec{F}_g$ as described above. Using Newton’s 2nd Law, we then have

$$\begin{aligned} \sum \vec{F} &= m\vec{a} \\ \vec{F}_g &= m\vec{a} \\ -\frac{GMm}{r^2}\, \hat{r} &= m\vec{a}. \end{aligned}$$

$\vec{a}$ might as well be written as $\mathrm{d}^2\vec{r}/\mathrm{d} t^2$. So we can now write

$$\begin{aligned} m\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \vec{r}}{\mathrm{d} t^2} &= -\frac{GMm}{r^2}\, \hat{r} \\[2pt] \frac{\mathrm{d}^2\vec{r}}{\mathrm{d} t^2} &= -\frac{GM}{r^2}\, \hat{r}. \end{aligned}$$

Notice that the planet’s mass $m$ cancelled clean off both sides! This tells us that the orbit doesn’t care how heavy the planet is, only how heavy the star is.

The whole essence of proving Kepler’s 1st Law is simply to solve this differential equation and show that the vector $\vec{r}$ traces out an ellipse over time, with the Sun at one of the foci of that ellipse.

3.1 Splitting It Into Components

A computer can’t do much with $\hat{r}$ directly, so let’s write everything out in coordinates.

The planet’s position is $(x,y)$, so $r^2 = x^2+y^2$, or $r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. We then see that the unit vector $\hat{r}$ has components $(x/r,\, y/r)$. You can verify yourself that this is indeed a unit vector with magnitude 1! So now we get two differential equations, one in $x$ and one in $y$:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 x}{\mathrm{d} t^2} = -\frac{GM}{r^2}\left( \frac{x}{r} \right) = -\frac{GM}{r^3}\,x$$
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 y}{\mathrm{d} t^2} = -\frac{GM}{r^2}\left( \frac{y}{r} \right) = -\frac{GM}{r^3}\,y.$$

Remember that these are two separate differential equations, with the $x$ and $y$ components of position each having their own solution. These two lines are the entire physics of our simulation, so keep them handy; we’ll be referring back to them a lot.

One thing to notice before we move on: these two equations are coupled. The $x$ equation contains $r$, and $r$ depends on $y$. So we can’t just solve one and then the other, we have to advance both at the same time.

4. Initial Conditions

Obviously, the planet simply doesn’t teleport into some idealized ellipse. Equations (1) and (2) describe every possible orbit around our star, from a tight little circle to a long skinny cigar. Which one we actually get is decided entirely by where we drop the planet and how hard we push it.

So the shape of the orbit comes out of the initial conditions rather than the force law, which means picking those conditions carefully is most of the work here.

4.1 Setting Up the Start

So first, suppose the Sun sits at the origin $(0,0)$ for simplicity. The planet starts a distance $x_0$ to the right of the origin, lying on the $x$-axis. And suppose also that we give the planet a little ‘kick’ directly upward, so it sets off with velocity $\vec{v_0} = (0, v_{y0})$. For simplicity, we’ll have our planet begin at the perihelion (the point of closest approach).

Keep in mind that we are developing Python code that keeps track of four key quantities: $x$, $y$, $v_x$, $v_y$. Even if you have no past computational background, I have faith that you will make this happen!

4.2 Where to Start It

Now, say we want an ellipse with a particular semi-major axis $a$ and a particular eccentricity $e$. From the Vectors & Ellipses section, the center of the ellipse sits a distance $c$ from the focus, and the far end is a distance $a$ from the center. So measuring from the focus, the near end of the ellipse sits at $a - c$, and since $e = c/a$ gives us $c = ae$, we have

$$r_p = a - c = a - ae = a(1-e).$$

Thus, our starting distance is pinned down:

$$\boxed{x_0 = a(1-e).}$$

Half of the job is now done: we know where to start the planet for a given $(a,e)$, and we know the kick points straight up. What we don’t know yet is how big that kick should be. Kicking it too hard or too gently can distort our desired parameters $(a, e)$ off the bat. Surprisingly, there’s only exactly one speed that gives us the ellipse we asked for.

Unfortunately, the hardest part about controlling the shape of the orbit in code is deriving a formula that gives you that correct initial velocity. That’s what the next section is for.

5. Derivation of the Vis-Viva Equation

The Vis-Viva equation gives us the speed of an orbiting body at any point of its orbit. Once we have it, we plug in $r = a(1-e)$ and read off the initial velocity kick $(0, v_{y0})$ that sets our planet into an elliptical orbit of semi-major axis $a$.

How do you want to take this one?

5.1 Specific Mechanical Energy

The total energy $(E)$ of the orbiting planet is a sum of its kinetic $(K)$ and potential $(U)$ energy,

$$E = K+U,$$

or

$$E = \frac{1}{2} mv^2 - \frac{GMm}{r}.$$

Every term here carries a factor of $m$, and as we just saw, the planet’s mass shouldn’t matter to the orbit anyway. So let’s divide it out. Dividing the above energy equation by $m$ gives us the specific mechanical energy $(\epsilon)$, which represents the energy per unit mass:

$$\epsilon = \frac{1}{2} v^2 - \frac{GM}{r}.$$

Because the total mechanical energy is conserved, the specific mechanical energy remains constant throughout the entirety of the orbit.

5.2 Comparing the Turning Points

For an elliptical orbit of semi-major axis $a$ and eccentricity $e$, let’s look at the two turning points where the velocity vector is perfectly perpendicular to the position vector. These points are at the perihelion (where we have initially placed the planet, closest point of approach, $r_p = a(1-e)$) and the aphelion (the point of farthest approach, $r_a = a(1+e)$).

Recall that the angular momentum vector has magnitude $L = mvr \sin \theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the momentum and position vectors. At both turning points $\theta = 90^\circ$, so $\sin\theta = 1$ and this collapses to just $L = mvr$. Because angular momentum is conserved (you showed on the 2nd Law page that gravity exerts no torque about the star!), we can equate the respective magnitudes at the perihelion and aphelion:

$$\begin{aligned} m r_a v_a &= mr_p v_p \\ r_a v_a &= r_p v_p \\ v_a &= v_p \left( \frac{r_p}{r_a}\right) = v_p \left( \frac{a(1-e)}{a(1+e)}\right) \\ v_a &= v_p \left( \frac{1-e}{1+e}\right). \end{aligned}$$

As we mentioned, the specific mechanical energy $\epsilon$ is constant throughout the orbit, so it must be equal at the perihelion and the aphelion:

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2} v_p^2 - \frac{GM}{r_p} &= \frac{1}{2}v_a^2 - \frac{GM}{r_a} \\[4pt] \frac{1}{2} v_p^2 - \frac{GM}{a(1-e)} &= \frac{1}{2} \left[ v_p \left( \frac{1-e}{1+e}\right)\right]^2 - \frac{GM}{a(1+e)}. \end{aligned}$$

Only one unknown is left in there. By isolating $v_p^2$, we find that

$$v^2_p = \frac{GM(1+e)}{a(1-e)}.$$

5.3 The Energy of an Orbit

We substitute this expression for $v^2_p$ back into the original specific energy evaluated at the perihelion point:

$$\begin{aligned} \epsilon &= \frac{1}{2}v_p^2 - \frac{GM}{r_p} \\[2pt] \epsilon &= \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{GM(1+e)}{a(1-e)}\right] - \frac{GM}{a(1-e)} \\[2pt] \epsilon &= \frac{GM}{a(1-e)} \left[ \frac{1+e}{2} - 1 \right] \\[2pt] \epsilon &= \frac{GM}{a(1-e)} \cdot \frac{e-1}{2}. \end{aligned}$$

The $(1-e)$ cancels against the $(e-1)$ up to a sign, and carrying out the algebra we obtain the result

$$\boxed{\epsilon = -\frac{GM}{2a}.}$$

This highlights a beautiful property of orbital mechanics: the total specific orbital energy depends strictly on the mass of the central star and the size of the orbit’s semi-major axis $(a)$, completely independent of the eccentricity $e$! A nearly circular orbit and a long skinny one with the same $a$ carry exactly the same energy per unit mass. It’s also the reason the Vis-Viva equation comes out as clean as it does.

The negative sign, by the way, is the signature of a bound orbit. A planet with $\epsilon \geq 0$ has passed the escape speed, and its path is no longer periodic.

5.4 Assembling the Equation

Now, we are in the position to assemble the Vis-Viva equation. We have two expressions for the same conserved quantity, so set them equal:

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2} v^2 -\frac{GM}{r} &= \epsilon \\[2pt] \frac{1}{2} v^2 -\frac{GM}{r} &= -\frac{GM}{2a}. \end{aligned}$$

After isolating $v$, we finally arrive at the Vis-Viva equation:

$$\boxed{v = \sqrt{GM \left( \frac{2}{r} - \frac{1}{a}\right)}}.$$

The Vis-Viva equation gives the magnitude of the velocity at any point of the planet’s orbit in terms of the semi-major axis $a$ and its variable orbit radius $r$. Notice that there’s no $e$ anywhere in it! It relates the speed to the current radius and the semi-major axis, and that’s all. Eccentricity never enters.

5.5 Application of the Vis-Viva Equation

So how does the eccentricity get into our simulation at all? Through the starting distance, and nowhere else.

Our initial velocity kick $(0, v_{y0})$ occurs at a position $x_0 = a(1-e)$ to the right of the Sun, and since the kick is entirely in the $y$-direction, $v_{y0}$ is the full speed at that moment. Plugging into the Vis-Viva equation, we obtain the long-desired result

$$v_{y0} = \sqrt{GM \left( \frac{2}{a(1-e)} - \frac{1}{a} \right)}$$
$$\boxed{v_{y0} = \sqrt{GM \left( \frac{1+e}{a(1-e)} \right)}.}$$

So $e$ shows up twice in our setup, and both times it’s an initial condition: once in $x_0 = a(1-e)$, and once in the kick above. Those two numbers are everything our code needs in order to produce the ellipse we asked for.

6. Euler’s Method

We have the physics and we have the initial conditions. The one thing missing is time. Equations (1) and (2) give us the planet’s acceleration right now, but what we actually want to plot is its position over a whole orbit. So we need a way to get from one to the other.

We want to plot the position over time, but in order to do so, we first need to find the velocity at each time during the orbit. Mathematically, let us see how this arises.

As an example, we use the acceleration in the $x$ direction $a_x$. Start with the definition of acceleration,

$$a_x = \frac{\mathrm{d} v_x}{\mathrm{d} t}.$$

Rearrange so that

$$\mathrm{d} v_x = a_x \mathrm{d} t.$$

Now, suppose that the velocity in the $x$ direction at time $t$ is $v_{x,i}$ and at time $t+\Delta t$ it is $v_{x,f}$. The change in velocity $\Delta v_{x} = v_{x,f} - v_{x,i}$ is $a_x \Delta t$, as suggested by the above equation. Rearranging, we find that

$$v_{x,f} = v_{x,i} + a_x \Delta t.$$

This is effectively how Euler’s method works! We start with some initial positions and velocities. Then, according to the differential equation, we calculate the instantaneous acceleration for a time $t$. We use that quantity of acceleration to calculate the next value of velocity at a time $t+\Delta t$. Since we have a small $\Delta t \sim \mathrm{d} t$, our calculations can be incredibly precise, because we update our values so often.

Now here is the natural next question: if we have the velocity for all the times $t$ in our period (obtained from the method shown above), how can the position be obtained next? Use the definition of velocity and the same thought process shown above to arrive at your conclusion.

6.1 The Four Update Rules

Okay, now that you’ve (hopefully) shown what was asked, we’ll have four relations that will be useful in our code:

$$\begin{aligned} v_{x,f} &= v_{x,i} + a_x \Delta t \\ v_{y,f} &= v_{y,i} + a_y \Delta t \\ x_f &= x_i + v_{x,f}\, \Delta t \\ y_f &= y_i + v_{y,f}\, \Delta t. \end{aligned}$$

Take a close look at those last two lines: the position update uses $v_{x,f}$ and $v_{y,f}$, the new velocities, not the old ones. So the order we do things inside our loop actually matters. Each time through, we compute the acceleration from the current position, then update the velocities, and only then update the positions using those brand-new velocities.

Do not skip past this one. If you update the position first, using the old velocity, the simulation slowly leaks energy and your “ellipse” spirals outward into a spring instead of closing up on itself. Updating the velocity first keeps the orbit stable over many periods, even with identical physics and an identical $\Delta t$.

7. Setting Up the Code

7.1 Methodology

The programming language we will be using to plot the elliptical orbit is Python! Python has many numerical applications in scientific computing, and you should try to get familiar with it if you’d like to work in STEM-related fields.

Here, we want to plot an arbitrary ellipse and control its semi-major axis and eccentricity.

We will be working in a Jupyter Notebook (a .ipynb file), where our code will be pieced up into seven main cells. A cell is just a block of code that you run on its own by pressing Shift+Enter. Cells share memory, so a variable you define in one is still around in the next, which lets us build the program in stages and check each stage before moving on.

Here are the cells in order:

  1. Packages
  2. Constants
  3. Orbital Parameters
  4. Initial Conditions (Perihelion)
  5. Time Setup
  6. Storage + Simulation Loop
  7. Plotting

Some of these cells will be either fully given, partially given, or you will have to figure them out on your own! Our overall goal for this step-by-step run-through is to plot the elliptical orbit of Mercury about the Sun.

One rule for the whole program: everything stays in SI units (meters, kilograms, seconds) until the very last plot. We convert to AU once, at the end, just for the axis labels.

At the end of the process, I’ll hand you a problem to try on your own, for a different planet in our solar system.

7.2.4 Initial Conditions (Perihelion)

As we’ve discussed, we want our elliptical orbit to begin at the perihelion (point of closest approach, along the $x$-axis), and using ellipse geometry, this point is $a(1-e)$ to the right of the Sun. We have to set up two coordinates for both the position and the velocity, so that’s four variables in total.

Three of them are pretty much free (think about what “on the $x$-axis” and “kicked straight up” mean for the components you aren’t using). The fourth is the initial velocity from Section 5.5, and you’ll want np.sqrt() for the square root.

7.2.5 Time Setup

We will run the simulation for one full orbit, so we need the period $T$.

The period of an ellipse squared is proportional to the cube of its semi-major axis with the given proportionality constant (as you should’ve discovered in the derivation of Kepler’s 3rd Law):

$$T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM} a^3.$$

Taking the square root on both sides yields

$$T = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{GM}} a^{3/2}.$$

Set this value of a period inside Python. Note that numpy already has $\pi$ built in as np.pi, so you don’t need to type out a decimal for it.

How our code will work is by using Euler’s method for times throughout our period, continuously updating our values of velocity and hence position to trace out an elliptical orbit.

Anyways, we’d like to sample about a thousand consecutive values of time throughout our period. Under the code which sets the value of the period, write

This is our tiny time-step by which we will update the position and velocity coordinates, and it’s the $\Delta t$ from Section 6. We have 1000 values of time per period. When graphing this, the path will trace out a smooth elliptical curve. The more time values you sample, the better approximation your curve will be. Think about why this is true.

Next, we will set the number of values $N$ of position and velocity we’d like in our arrays (I will get to this in a moment). This should be the same amount of values as the number of time steps, 1000. Set this up beneath the dt code.

7.2.6 Storage + Simulation Loop

This is the interesting part, because now we have to write up Euler’s method for the differential equations (1) and (2), using the four update rules we found in Section 6.

First, let’s create arrays of $x$ and $y$, all filled with zeros. Arrays are basically fixed-length rows of numbers that Python can do math on all at once. We do this so that our code has somewhere to put the real values as it computes them; without this base array, our code would have no idea what to fill! We will have $N$ values of both $x$ and $y$, for $N$ time steps.

Write this in a new cell of your code:

This creates two arrays, both with $N$ zeros. This is our Storage.

Make sure you separate two things here, because this is where people tend to get stuck. The variables x and y hold where the planet is right now, and they get overwritten on every single step. The arrays xs and ys are the permanent record of everywhere it has been. We need both: the current position to compute the next step, and the full history to draw the orbit at the end.

Now let’s develop the Simulation Loop in a new cell of code. We are in the closing stretch!

Start with the following code. I will explain soon.

This loop runs through all $N$ time steps. range(N) means the counter i takes the values $0, 1, 2, \dots, N-1$, so the indented lines run $N$ times, once per step. At each step i, it takes the current position of the planet (x and y) and stores it into the i-th slot of our arrays. So xs[0] gets the planet’s starting $x$ position, xs[1] gets the next one, and so on, all the way up to xs[N-1]. The same idea applies for the $y$ coordinate. (Python starts counting slots at 0 rather than 1, so watch out for that.)

A few pointers to keep you on track:

  • r is the planet’s current distance from the Sun, and you’ve got x and y.
  • ax and ay come straight out of equations (1) and (2). They need r, which is why r gets computed first.
  • For the velocities, something like vx = vx + ax * dt means “take the old vx, add $a_x \Delta t$, and store the answer back in vx.” In Python this is an instruction rather than an equation, and it’s exactly our $v_{x,f} = v_{x,i} + a_x \Delta t$ rule.
  • Remember from Section 6 that the position updates use the velocities we just calculated. The skeleton above is already in the right order, so don’t rearrange it.

Vectors & Ellipses

Abir Mehta

The 2nd and 3rd Law derivations build on a few math ideas: vectors, the cross product, the dot product, and the geometry of an ellipse. None of it is particularly challenging, but dropping it in the middle of a physics derivation just gets in the way. So everything sits here on its own page. Read the tidbits you need, then jump back to whichever law you were working on.

Note that one thing we are not doing on this page is proving that orbits are ellipses in the first place. That’s Kepler’s 1st Law, and it’s a separate derivation. Here we just need to know what an ellipse is so the rest makes sense.

1. Vectors

A vector is just a quantity with both a magnitude and a direction. Velocity is a vector (50 km/h, heading north); so is force, and so is position. We draw one as an arrow: the length is the magnitude, and the way it points is the direction. We write vectors with a little arrow on top, like $\vec{A}$, and the plain symbol $A$ (no arrow) means just the magnitude.

A unit vector is a vector whose length is exactly $1$. All it tells you is direction. We put a hat on it instead of an arrow, like $\hat{r}$. Unit vectors are handy because any vector can be split into “how long” times “which way”: for example, $\vec{r} = r\hat{r}$ means “a distance $r$ in the $\hat{r}$ direction.” This is the notation we’ll work with in the 2nd Law setup.

2. The Vector Cross Product

The vector cross product may seem like a tricky concept, but its physical meaning is more fundamental to understanding it than the math itself.

Suppose, we have two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. Their cross product $\vec{A} \times \vec{B}$ is another vector $\vec{C}$. $\vec{C}$ has magnitude $|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|\sin \theta_{AB}$ where $\theta_{AB}$ is the angle between vector $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. More importantly, however, $\vec{C}$ is mutually perpendicular (orthogonal) to both $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. Not sure what that looks like? Check out the figure below!

Note that if $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are parallel or anti-parallel, then $\theta_{AB} = 0$ or $\pi$, so $|\vec{C}| = |\vec{A}||\vec{B}|\sin \theta_{AB} = 0$. In other words, the cross product of two aligned vectors is always zero.

3. The Dot Product

The dot product is the other way to multiply two vectors. Just like with the cross product, understanding what it represents matters more than the formula itself.

Suppose, we have two vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. Their dot product $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}$ is a scalar—just a number, not a vector. It is equal to $|\vec{A}||\vec{B}|\cos \theta_{AB}$ where $\theta_{AB}$ is the angle between vector $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$. Notice that when $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ point in the same direction, $\theta_{AB} = 0$, so $\cos \theta_{AB} = 1$ and the dot product is at its largest. When they are perpendicular, $\theta_{AB} = 90^\circ$, so $\cos \theta_{AB} = 0$ and the dot product is zero. Not sure what that looks like? Check out the figure below!

Note that this is the opposite of the cross product: the dot product is zero when the two vectors are perpendicular, while the cross product is zero when they are parallel.

4. Ellipses

You’ve worked with circles forever, but ellipses probably haven’t gotten as much attention—and Kepler’s laws are full of them so let’s try to get familiar with one. The good news is that an ellipse is basically a stretched-out circle.

4.1 The two-thumbtack definition

Pick two fixed points and call them the foci (one focus, two foci). An ellipse is every point whose distances to those two foci add up to the same total. There’s a classic way to see this: take a loop of string, pin it down at two spots with thumbtacks, pull it tight with a pencil, and trace all the way around. Since the string length never changes, the two distances always add up to the same length, and you get a perfect ellipse. Check out the figure below!

Why should we care? It’s because of where the Sun sits. In Kepler’s 1st Law, a planet orbits in an ellipse with the Sun at one of the foci—not at the center. That’s exactly why a planet gets close to the Sun on one side of its orbit and swings far away on the other.

4.2 The vocabulary ($a$, $b$, $c$, and $e$)

Put the ellipse flat with its long direction along the $x$-axis and its center at the origin. There are four key lengths that we’ll discuss. The semi-major axis $a$ is the distance from the center out to the far end—the long way. The semi-minor axis $b$ is the distance from the center out to the side—the short way. The distance $c$ tells you how far each focus sits from the center. And the eccentricity $e = c/a$ is a single number for how squished the ellipse is: $e = 0$ gives a perfect circle, and as $e$ gets closer to $1$ the ellipse stretches out longer and skinnier.

4.3 Let’s check a couple of these

First up: the two distances always add to $2a$. To see it, slide your point all the way to the right end of the ellipse. From there, the distance to the far focus is the whole width minus a little, and the distance to the near focus is that little bit—add them and you just get the full width, which is $2a$. Since the total is fixed for every point, we get

$$r_1 + r_2 = 2a$$

for any point on the ellipse.

Next, the relationship between $a$, $b$, and $c$. Move your point up to the very top of the ellipse. By symmetry it’s the same distance from both foci, and since those distances add to $2a$, each one is exactly $a$. Now look at the triangle made by the center, one focus, and that top point: its legs are $b$ and $c$, and its hypotenuse is $a$. Using Pythagorean theorem, gives us

$$a^2 = b^2 + c^2.$$

4.4 Where the equation comes from

If you want the actual equation of the ellipse, put the foci at $(-c, 0)$ and $(c, 0)$ and write the definition out for a point $(x, y)$:

$$\sqrt{(x+c)^2 + y^2} + \sqrt{(x-c)^2 + y^2} = 2a.$$

It looks messy, but it’s just algebra: move one square root over, square both sides, simplify, isolate the other square root, and square again. You end up with

$$\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{a^2 - c^2} = 1,$$

and since we just showed $a^2 - c^2 = b^2$, that’s the standard form:

$$\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1.$$

Quick check: if you set $a = b$ (so $c = 0$ and both foci land on the center), this turns into $x^2 + y^2 = a^2$—just a circle of radius $a$. So a circle really is an ellipse with $e = 0$, which is exactly why we’re allowed to use a circle as the easy case when we derive Kepler’s 3rd Law.

Kepler’s Second Law: Derivation

Abir Mehta

1. What is Kepler’s 2nd Law?

Kepler’s 2nd Law states that an imaginary line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Refer to Fig. 1 for a visual representation of the law.

At first, this seems so abstract. How would you even measure areas swept out, especially on an ellipse—such a weird shape? Well think about it like this: in a time $\Delta t$, the planet should sweep out an area $\Delta A$ relative to its Sun that sits at one of the foci. If Kepler’s 2nd Law holds, then the quantity $\Delta A /\Delta t$ should remain constant, no matter how small or large the time interval $\Delta t$ is. And $\Delta A /\Delta t$ is really just the change in area over the change in time—which is exactly what differentiation measures! So we can write it as a derivative,

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} \;\; \text{should remain constant!}$$

Now, we’ve reduces Kepler’s 2nd Law from an unintuitive representation to something we can mathematically work with! Sounds pretty cool!

Understanding Kepler’s 2nd Law is only the first step; we need to go deeper into the background information!

2. Background Information

2.1 Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation: Vector Form

I’m sure you guys have heard of Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation, but only represented in magnitudes:

$$F_g = \frac{GMm}{r^2}.$$

Pretty familiar right? Well here is the vector form:

$$\vec{F}_g = -\frac{GMm}{r^2} \hat{r}.$$

The vector form of Newton’s universal law of gravitation simply gives both the magnitude and direction of the force of gravity acting on mass $m$ due to mass $M$. Here, $r$ is the distance between the two masses measured along the line connecting them. We assume that the mass $M$ is fixed in place for simplicity (though this is not exactly true if you want to do some further digging).

Okay, there might be a few things going through your mind: what is that little hat doing on the $r$? what do you mean by a “line connecting them”? where does the negative sign pop up from? If the hat notation is new to you, the Vectors & Ellipses tab has you covered—here we’ll just look at what it means for gravity. Let’s break it down with an illustration!

The symbol $\hat{r}$ is a unit vector pointing along the line connecting $M$ and $m$. Key distinction: it points from $M$ to to $m$. Its direction continuously changes as $m$ moves relative to $M$.

In the context of classical mechanics (as you may have been taught), gravity is a central force that’s also an “action-at-a-distance”. As shown in Fig. 2, we place our central body $M$ at the origin, so $\hat{r}$ points away from $M$. But the force of gravity on $m$ pulls it toward $M$—the opposite direction. That’s where the negative sign comes from! Our vector form

$$\vec{F}_g = -\frac{GMm}{r^2} \hat{r}$$

takes a step in the right direction ;) which is good! Well, what about the magnitude? Well because $\hat{r}$ is a unit vector, the magnitude of $\vec{F}_g$ is again $GMm/r^2$. This aligns exactly with the ‘magnitude-only’ form you were taught earlier.

Make you understand Newton’s Universal Law of Gravitation in its vector form, because it is vital first step for the derivation.

The other tool we’ll need is the vector cross product, since that’s how torque is defined. I’ve put the full explanation over on the Vectors & Ellipses tab to keep this page focused—give it a look if you need a refresher.

3. Deriving Kepler’s 2nd Law

3.1 The Setup

Suppose we have a large mass $M$ fixed at the origin of our coordinate system. Compared to $m$, its tiny revolutions about the system’s center of mass are negligible—so we treat it as stationary. The mass $m$ follows an elliptical orbit about $M$, which sits at one of the foci.

We can describe the position of $m$ at any moment with a position vector $\vec{r}(t)$, which gives both the direction and distance of $m$ from the origin. Since $\vec{r}(t)$ points along our familiar unit vector $\hat{r}$ and has magnitude $r$ (the distance between $M$ and $m$), we can write $\vec{r}(t) = r\hat{r}$.

In terms of cross products, the vector form of torque $\vec{\tau}$ is defined as

$$\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}.$$

Notice how this aligns with the typical formula for torque that deals with magnitudes:

$$\tau = rF \sin \theta.$$

Refer back to the cross product section (on the Vectors & Ellipses tab) if you are confused.

Derivation · one step at a time
Step 1: Angular Momentum Conservation

And once you have that, what does it tell you about the magnitude of its angular momentum, $L$, about $M$ as it orbits?

4. Result

You should arrive at

$$\boxed{\frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{L}{2m}.}$$

And there it is—Kepler’s 2nd Law, derived straight from Newton’s law of gravitation! Look at what’s left on the right side. $L$ is conserved, which is exactly what we showed back in Step 1, and $m$ is just the planet’s mass, which certainly isn’t going anywhere. A constant over a constant is a constant, so $\mathrm{d}A/\mathrm{d}t$ never changes, and the planet really does sweep out equal areas in equal times.

Notice what we never once needed: the orbit being an ellipse. The only thing this derivation leans on is that gravity is a central force—it points straight along $\vec{r}$, so it exerts no torque about $M$. Any central force at all would give you the same law. Pretty cool, right?

So why does a planet speed up near the Sun?

This is the part of the 2nd Law you can actually picture. We found that $r^2\,\mathrm{d}\theta/\mathrm{d}t$ has to stay fixed, so if $r$ shrinks, $\mathrm{d}\theta/\mathrm{d}t$ has no choice but to grow. Near the perihelion the planet is close in, so it has to swing around quickly; out at the aphelion it is far away and can afford to crawl. Same swept area either way—a short fat wedge near the Sun, a long skinny one far from it.

Mercury is the showy example: it moves at about $59\ \mathrm{km/s}$ at perihelion and only $39\ \mathrm{km/s}$ at aphelion. You get to watch this happen for yourself when you simulate its orbit over on the 1st Law page.

Kepler’s Third Law: Derivation

Abir Mehta

1. What is Kepler’s 3rd Law?

Okay, last one! Kepler’s 3rd Law states that the square of a planet’s orbital period $T$ is proportional to the cube of its semi-major axis $a$:

$$T^2 \propto a^3.$$

If the term “semi-major axis” is unfamiliar, no worries—you can find a full breakdown of what $a$ means over on the Vectors & Ellipses tab. For a circular orbit, though, it’s nothing complicated: $a$ is just the radius!

So what does this law actually tell us? The farther a planet is from the Sun, the longer its orbital period—that part you could probably guess. But the period doesn’t grow proportionally with distance. Push a planet out to twice the orbital size and its period doesn’t just double, it stretches by a factor of $2\sqrt{2} \approx 2.83$! Kepler uncovered this pattern by poring over Brahe’s data, and now we get to derive it ourselves from Newton’s mechanics. Pretty cool, right?

We’ll derive it for the simplest case: a perfectly circular orbit, where the semi-major axis $a$ is just the radius $r$. The same result holds for elliptical orbits too, but proving that needs the full orbit equation, which is a bit beyond our scope here.

2. Deriving Kepler’s 3rd Law

2.1 The Setup

Our setup is similar to the 2nd Law: a large mass $M$ fixed at the origin, with a small mass $m$ orbiting around it. The only difference this time is that $m$ moves along a circular orbit of radius $r$.

Gravity is still the only force acting on $m$, and we know its magnitude:

$$F_g = \frac{GMm}{r^2}.$$

Now, for a circular orbit, gravity always points directly toward the center—and that’s exactly the direction you need to keep something moving in a circle! In other words, gravity supplies the centripetal force that keeps the planet in its orbit. That’s the fact we’ll build the derivation on.

Derivation · one step at a time
Step 1: Gravity as the Centripetal Force

Since gravity is the only force acting on $m$ and it points straight at the center, it must be the centripetal force holding $m$ in its circular orbit. Using what you know about uniform circular motion, set gravity equal to the centripetal force. What do you get?

Quick refresher from circular motion: to keep a mass $m$ moving in a circle of radius $r$ at speed $v$, you need a centripetal force $F_c = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.

Hint 2: Step 1≈60%

Now just set the gravitational force equal to the centripetal force:

$$\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}.$$
Hint 3: Step 1≈85%

Notice that there’s an $m$ on both sides—so it cancels! (Neat side effect: the orbit doesn’t depend on the planet’s mass at all, only on $M$.) Cancel the $m$ and multiply both sides by $r$.

Answer100%

After simplifying, you should have

$$\frac{GM}{r} = v^2.$$
Step 2: Get rid of the speed

Nice! But that result still has $v$ in it, and Kepler’s law is about the period $T$, not the speed. So let’s get rid of $v$. Think about it: in one full period $T$, the planet travels exactly once around the circle. Can you write $v$ in terms of $r$ and $T$?

Step 3

Home stretch! Rearrange the equation from Step 2 to solve for $T^2$. Once it’s isolated, take a good look—what’s the relationship between $T$ and $r$? No hints for this one, you’ve got it!

3. Result

You should arrive at

$$\boxed{T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM} r^3.}$$

And there it is—Kepler’s 3rd Law, derived straight from Newton’s law of gravitation! Notice the constant out front, $4\pi^2/(GM)$: it depends only on the central mass $M$, not on the orbiting planet. This means every planet orbiting the same Sun shares the same value of $T^2/r^3$. Kepler spotted this pattern just by studying Brahe’s data; Newton’s mechanics is what finally explains why it’s true.

Does this actually hold for ellipses?

We pulled this off for a circle, where $a = r$. But real planets move on ellipses—so does the law survive? It does! All you do is trade the radius $r$ for the semi-major axis $a$, and it reads

$$T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM} a^3,$$

same constant out front, same $T^2 \propto a^3$. The honest catch is that nailing this down for a general ellipse takes the full orbit equation, which is more than we want to get into here. If you want to see the elliptical case worked all the way through, Taylor’s Classical Mechanics (§8.5–8.6) is a great place to look.

Extension Problem

Sofia Gainullina & Adar Özalkak

Introduction

In this problem you will work with the remarkably precise planetary position data set recorded by Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe without a telescope from 1582 to 1600 CE to understand the relationship between Earth-based observations of planetary positions, their heliocentric orbits, Kepler’s empirically derived Laws of Planetary Motion, and Newton’s explanatory Law of Universal Gravitation.

Part 1

Background

Kepler’s Laws demonstrated that planets follow elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus, and Newton’s Law of Universal Gravitation provided a theoretical framework for why these orbits must be ellipses.

Before we get there, however, we are going to start by understanding the mathematical conversion between the declination of Mars as observed from Brahe’s observatory on the island of Hven, 55.90778° N latitude and 12.69667° E longitude, and the position vector of Mars relative to the Earth as viewed in the “universe frame” in which we are looking at the orbits of Mars and Earth around the Sun.

Start with the following assumptions; we will iteratively improve the model over the course of this problem.

  • Both Earth and Mars are in circular orbits about the Sun, which is at the center of each orbit.
  • The orbits of Earth and Mars are co-planar.
  • Both Earth and Mars are orbiting the Sun at constant speed.

Vectors can be added head-to-tail to represent a sequence of motion or displacement.

3. Circular Motion

Let’s say

  • $r_M$: the radius of Mars’ orbit.
  • $\omega_M$: the angular speed of Mars’ orbit.
  • $r_E$: the radius of Earth’s orbit.
  • $\omega_E$: the angular speed of Earth’s orbit.
  • $t$: the time that has passed since a starting point at which both Earth and Mars are on the $x$-axis.

Assign a two-dimensional Cartesian coordinate system to your diagram, and write the components of all three vectors in terms of $r_M$, $\omega_M$, $r_E$, $\omega_E$, and $t$. If you are stuck, reveal the hints below!

Work it out · one hint at a time
0 / 4
0% of the solution revealed
Hint 1≈22%

Suppose a planet is moving around a circle of radius $r$, and its angular position is $\theta$. If the Sun is at the origin, how can you express the planet’s $x$- and $y$-coordinates in terms of $r$ and $\theta$?

Hint 2≈48%

Recall that in a right triangle,

$$\cos\theta = \frac{x}{r}, \qquad \sin\theta = \frac{y}{r}.$$

How can we write $x$ and $y$ in terms of $\cos\theta$, $\sin\theta$, and $r$? Rewriting the above-mentioned equations leads us to

$$x = r\cos\theta \qquad \text{and} \qquad y = r\sin\theta.$$
Hint 3≈72%

Consider Mars. Its angular speed is $\omega_M$, so after time $t$, what is its angular position $\theta_M$?

Use the same idea for Earth. Its angular speed is $\omega_E$, so what is its angular position $\theta_E$?

Answer100%

Once you have the coordinates of Earth and Mars, note that rearranging the result from Problem 2, we have

$$\mathbf{r_{ME}} = \mathbf{r_{MS}} - \mathbf{r_{ES}}.$$

Can you use this to find the components of $\mathbf{r_{ME}}$?

If a point is moving on a circle of radius $r$ with angular position $\theta$, its Cartesian coordinates are

$$x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta.$$

Since both planets begin on the $x$-axis and move with constant angular speed, their angular positions after time $t$ are

$$\theta_M = \omega_M t$$

for Mars, and

$$\theta_E = \omega_E t$$

for Earth.

Therefore, the position vector of Mars relative to the Sun is

$$\mathbf{r_{MS}}(t) = \langle r_M\cos(\omega_M t),\, r_M\sin(\omega_M t)\rangle$$

and the position vector of Earth relative to the Sun is

$$\mathbf{r_{ES}}(t) = \langle r_E\cos(\omega_E t),\, r_E\sin(\omega_E t)\rangle.$$

Problem 2 tells us that

$$\mathbf{r_{ES}} + \mathbf{r_{ME}} = \mathbf{r_{MS}},$$

which can be rewritten as

$$\mathbf{r_{ME}} = \mathbf{r_{MS}} - \mathbf{r_{ES}}.$$

Substituting our expressions yields

$$\mathbf{r_{ME}}(t) = \langle r_M\cos(\omega_M t),\, r_M\sin(\omega_M t)\rangle - \langle r_E\cos(\omega_E t),\, r_E\sin(\omega_E t)\rangle,$$

and subtracting the components gives

$$\mathbf{r_{ME}}(t) = \langle r_M\cos(\omega_M t) - r_E\cos(\omega_E t),\; r_M\sin(\omega_M t) - r_E\sin(\omega_E t)\rangle.$$

Thus, we’ve written the components of all three vectors in terms of the given values.
